name: Black Cultural Archives
text: Your train passes near the Black Cultural Archives, on the train's {side}, founded in 1981 by the historian Len Garrison and others to record the history of people of African and Caribbean descent in Britain. Since 2014 it has been at Raleigh Hall, a Georgian building on Windrush Square.

name: Brixton Market
text: Your train passes near Brixton Market, on the train's {side}, which began on Atlantic Road in the 1870s and is best known for its African and Caribbean food. Electric Avenue, now part of the market, was built in the 1880s as one of the first streets with electric light, and is the street in Eddy Grant's song.

name: Ark Evelyn Grace Academy
text: Your train passes near Ark Evelyn Grace Academy, on the train's {side}, a secondary school whose building, designed by Zaha Hadid, won the Stirling Prize in 2011. The sweeping Z-shaped building opened in 2010, and the grounds include a 100-metre running track.

name: King's College Hospital
text: Your train passes near King's College Hospital, on the train's {side}, a teaching hospital and major trauma centre that began in 1840 in a disused workhouse near Lincoln's Inn Fields. It moved to a greenfield site here at Denmark Hill in 1913, and Queen Camilla was born there.

name: The Rose
text: Your train passes near the site of the Rose, on the train's {side}, the playhouse Philip Henslowe built on Bankside in 1587. Two of Shakespeare's earliest plays, Titus Andronicus and Henry VI, Part 1, are recorded as being performed there, and its remains were found in 1989 when an office block was being built.

name: The George Inn
text: Your train passes near the George Inn, on the train's {side}, the only galleried coaching inn left in London, owned by the National Trust. It was rebuilt in 1677 after a fire; the Great Northern Railway later used it as a depot and pulled down two of its fronts, so only the south side survives.

name: Borough Market
text: Your train passes Borough Market, on the train's {side}, one of the oldest food markets in London: there has been a market on the site since at least the 12th century. The present buildings date from the 1850s, and today it mainly sells speciality food.

name: Menier Chocolate Factory
text: Your train passes near the Menier Chocolate Factory, on the train's {side}, a 180-seat theatre opened in 2004 behind a factory the French Menier chocolate company built between 1865 and 1874. Its production of Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George won five Olivier Awards in 2007.

name: St Mary's Church, Croydon
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, on the train's {side}, a Catholic church in the Gothic Revival style built in 1863 and 1864 to designs by E. W. Pugin and Frederick Walters. Its site was bought in 1861 for £742.

name: Warehouse Theatre
text: Your train passes the site of the Warehouse Theatre, on the train's {side}, a 100-seat theatre in a Victorian cement warehouse, whose first play opened in May 1977. Known for new writing, it closed in 2012, and the building was pulled down in 2013.

name: The Four Aces Club
text: Your train passes the site of the Four Aces Club, on the train's {side}, which in the 1960s and 1970s was one of the first venues in Britain to play black music, with Bob Marley, Stevie Wonder and Jimmy Cliff among its visitors. The Prodigy played their first live show there; the building was pulled down in 2007.

name: Balls Pond Road Cemetery
text: Your train passes Balls Pond Road Cemetery, on the train's {side}, a Jewish burial ground founded in 1843 and owned by West London Synagogue. The ashes of Amy Levy, the first Jewish woman to be cremated in England, are here; the last burial was in 1951.

name: Trinity Green Almshouses
text: Your train passes near Trinity Green Almshouses, on the train's {side}, built in 1695 by Trinity House for 28 retired masters and commanders of ships, or their widows. In the 1890s a campaign led by C. R. Ashbee saved them from being pulled down.

name: St John on Bethnal Green
text: Your train passes near St John on Bethnal Green, on the train's {side}, a church built between 1826 and 1828 to the design of Sir John Soane. Inside are 14 Stations of the Cross by the painter Chris Gollon, commissioned in 2000.

name: Copper Box Arena
text: Your train passes near the Copper Box Arena, on the train's {side}, built for the 2012 Olympics as the Handball Arena and renamed in January 2012 to suit its look. As well as handball, it held modern pentathlon events at the Olympics and goalball at the Paralympics.

name: Lewisham Road station
text: Your train passes near the old Lewisham Road station, on the train's {side}, opened in 1871 by the London, Chatham and Dover Railway on its branch from Nunhead to Greenwich Park. The branch closed in 1917 as a wartime economy, but the station building on Loampit Hill still stands.

name: Ladywell Fields
text: Your train passes Ladywell Fields, on the train's {side}, a park made from three historic fields, recorded as meadows in the Domesday Book. A well first recorded in 1472, and said to cure eye complaints, now lies under the road to Ladywell station.

name: Lewisham Odeon
text: Your train passes the site of the Lewisham Odeon, on the train's {side}, which opened in 1932 as the Gaumont Palace with 3,050 seats, one of the largest cinemas in Britain. The Beatles and the Rolling Stones played there; it closed on February 14th 1981 and was pulled down in 1991 to widen the road.

name: St Saviour's Church, Lewisham
text: Your train passes near St Saviour's Church, on the train's {side}, a Catholic church on Lewisham High Street built in 1898 in the Italianate style, with an interior of coloured marble.

name: Grove Park Nature Reserve
text: Your train passes Grove Park Nature Reserve, on the train's {side}, woodland and meadow beside the line. From 1894 to 1899 Edith Nesbit lived in a house on Baring Road whose garden backed onto the railway here, and the path to the reserve is called Railway Children Walk.

name: Hither Green Cemetery
text: Your train passes near Hither Green Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1873 as Lee Cemetery, although Lee's church is about 1.5 miles away. It was designed by Francis Freeman Thorne, who is buried there, with two Gothic chapels by William Webster.

name: University House
text: Your train passes near University House, on the train's {side}, built from 1898 as the West Ham Technical Institute, with carved figures for art, science, literature, engineering and music. At its opening in 1900 John Passmore Edwards called it a “people's university”; it is now part of the University of East London.

name: St Mary's Church, Little Ilford
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Little Ilford, on the train's {side}, which is mainly 12th century, with a chapel for the Lethieullier family added in 1724. It is listed at Grade I.

name: Crayford Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Crayford Town Hall, on the train's {side}, built in red brick in 1915 as the canteen for the Vickers armaments factory. After the First World War the factory shrank, and in 1929 the council bought the building for its offices.

name: Orchard Theatre, Dartford
text: Your train passes near the Orchard Theatre, on the train's {side}, a 1,025-seat theatre built by Dartford Borough Council and opened by the Duke of Kent on April 14th 1983. It closed in September 2023 over concerns about RAAC concrete in its structure, and its shows moved to a temporary venue.

name: Sharnbrook Summit
text: Your train passes Sharnbrook Summit, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve on a mile-long strip of grassland above a railway tunnel. It grows on limestone left when the railway was built, with tor-grass, dyer's greenweed and wild liquorice.

name: Katherine cross
text: Your train passes near the Katherine cross, on the train's {side}, put up in Ampthill Park in 1773 by the Earl of Upper Ossory on the site of Ampthill Castle, where Katherine of Aragon was confined in 1533. It carries an inscription by Horace Walpole.

name: Harlington Manor
text: Your train passes near Harlington Manor, on the train's {side}, a Grade II* listed manor house overlooking the village common. In November 1660 John Bunyan was questioned here by Sir Francis Wingate and held briefly in the house, before being sent to prison in Bedford for the next 12 years.

name: Waulud's Bank
text: Your train passes near Waulud's Bank, on the train's {side}, a D-shaped earthwork from around 3000 BC, with the River Lea, which rises nearby, along one side. Its shape is almost the same as that of Marden Henge in Wiltshire.

name: Kenilworth Road
text: Your train passes near Kenilworth Road, on the train's {side}, home of Luton Town since 1905. Its record crowd of 30,069 came in 1959, and in September 2023 it held its first Premier League match, against West Ham United.

name: St Mary's Church, Luton
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Luton, on the train's {side}, built by Robert, Earl of Gloucester, from 1121 and consecrated in 1137. One of the largest churches in Bedfordshire, it is the only Grade I listed building in Luton.

name: Luton Hoo
text: Your train passes the park of Luton Hoo, on the train's {side}, which Capability Brown enlarged from about 300 acres to 1,200 while Robert Adam was working on the house. Brown dammed the River Lea to make two lakes.

name: Beech Bottom Dyke
text: Your train passes Beech Bottom Dyke, on the train's {side}, a great ditch with banks on both sides that runs for almost a mile along the northern edge of St Albans. It was dug at the end of the Iron Age, probably in the first half of the first century AD, and carries on beyond the railway embankment.

name: Napsbury Hospital
text: Your train passes the grounds of the former Napsbury Hospital, on the train's {side}, which opened in 1905 as the Middlesex County Asylum, with parkland laid out by William Goldring. The artist Louis Wain was a patient; the hospital closed in 1998, and the site is now the Napsbury Park housing.

name: Brunton Memorial Ground
text: Your train passes Brunton Memorial Ground, on the train's {side}, the home of Radlett Cricket Club, with the railway along its eastern edge. It is named after Miles Brunton, who bought the ground and leased it to the club for 99 years, and Middlesex have played county matches here since 2013.

name: Caldwell Priory
text: Your train passes near the site of Caldwell Priory, on the train's {side}, a house of the Canons of the Holy Sepulchre founded in the 12th century on the south bank of the Great Ouse. It was surrendered in 1536, when the smaller monasteries were closed.

name: Moot Hall, Elstow
text: Your train passes near the Moot Hall at Elstow, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed market hall built around 1500 to serve Elstow Abbey, and now a museum. John Bunyan, who was born in the village, developed his nonconformist ideas here in the mid-17th century.

name: Stewartby
text: Your train passes near Stewartby, on the train's {side}, a model village begun in 1926 for workers of the London Brick Company and named in 1936 after the company's Stewart family. The brickworks closed in 2008, and its last four chimneys came down on September 26th 2021.

name: Forest of Marston Vale
text: Your train passes the Forest of Marston Vale, on the train's {side}, a community forest planted across land left by brickmaking, where some of the empty clay pits are now lakes. Its Millennium Country Park, opened in 2000, includes the large Stewartby Lake.

name: Millbrook Proving Ground
text: Your train passes near Millbrook Proving Ground, on the train's {side}, one of the largest vehicle testing centres in Europe, opened in 1970. Bedford, General Motors' British company, built it on the pattern of GM's Milford Proving Ground in Michigan.
